newsitem.title: BRAZIL: HSBC takes over Brazil's Bamerindus.
newsitem.headline: HSBC takes over Brazil's Bamerindus.

text.p: Hong Kong & Shanghai Banking Corp. Wednesday bought failed Banco Bamerindus for 400 million reais ($377 million), ending months of speculation over the fate of Brazil's fourth largest private bank.

HSBC, which already owned a minority stake in Bamerindus, will assume the bank's selected assets and liabilities, valued at 10 billion reais ($9.4 billion), and turn it into a new bank with an immediate $1 billion ($940 million) capital injection.

Late Wednesday, Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso signed a decree approving HSBC's takeover of Bamerindus as required by the Constitution regarding acquisition of a Brazilian bank by a foreign institution.
The new bank, which Central Bank officials said is likely to be called HSBC-Bamerindus, will honour all Bamerindus' international obligations and credit.

Bamerindus, which since early last year had been plagued by rumours it would be sold due to its widely known liquidity troubles, is considered the last of Brazil's large private banks that needed restructuring.
In 1995, the Central Bank brokered a similar deal allowing the takeover of the healthy portion of failed bank Banco Nacional by private bank Unibanco.
Early last year, the Central Bank announced the acquisition of failed Banco Economico by Excel Banco. Economico and Nacional were among Brazil's top 10 financial institutions.

Like most Brazilian banks, Bamerindus suffered from the effects of the 32-month-old Real stabilisation plan, which slashed inflation and virtually eliminated banks' almost risk-free profits earned on wide arbitrage spreads.
The result has been the abrupt closure of many smaller and less competitive financial institutions.
Bamerindus' investment in the pulp and paper sector with the creation of its subsidiary Inpacel, which drowned in debts, was also seen as one of the bank's biggest headaches.

A solution for Bamerindus had been delayed for months on the insistence of controlling majority shareholder Jose Eduardo Andrade Vieira, a powerful senator and government ally, that he remain in charge.

With the takeover deal, Andrade Vieira's assets will be frozen as required by law until what was left of Bamerindus and remained in Central Bank's hands is liquidated or when all of the old bank's liabilities are paid off.
By acquiring Bamerindus, HSBC moves to strenghten its presence in Brazil, one of the world's fastest-growing emerging markets.
